extracted.intended_audience: analysts and rulewriters in U.S. Federal agencies preparing regulatory analyses and supporting materials for OMB/OIRA review
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing regulatory analyses for economically significant and other major federal rulemakings, including benefit-cost and cost-effectiveness analyses, accounting statements, and specialized statutory analyses. Focused on methods, documentation, alternatives, uncertainty treatment, and required ancillary analyses (RFA, NEPA, Paperwork Reduction Act, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Key Elements of a Regulatory Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: A good regulatory analysis should include: (1) a statement of the need for the proposed action, (2) an examination of alternative approaches, and (3) an evaluation of the benefits and costs—quantitative and qualitative—of the proposed action and the main alternatives identified by the analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three elements form the backbone of analysis; include linkage from rule actions to expected benefits, a clearly stated baseline, and identification of ancillary effects. Produce summaries (including standardized accounting statement) and appendices documenting models and data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of the Need for Federal Regulatory Action
rubrics_metrics.description: Before recommending Federal regulatory action, an agency must demonstrate that the proposed action is necessary, identify the specific problem to be addressed, and describe the statutory authority and extent of discretion available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain whether the action addresses market failures or other compelling public needs, demonstrate that federal action is likely to do more good than harm, and discuss strengths and limitations of intangible rationales when used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate Market Failure or Other Social Purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: If relying on market failure as justification, identify the type (externality, market power, inadequate/asymmetric information) and describe it qualitatively and where feasible quantitatively; other justifications (improving government functioning, redistribution, anti-discrimination, privacy) should also be examined for effectiveness and cost-effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume the mere possibility of market failure is sufficient—document its existence and relevance carefully; consider alternatives to regulation appropriate to the failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show Federal Level is Appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether alternatives to Federal regulation (antitrust, litigation, State/local regulation, administrative compensation) could address the problem more efficiently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine geographic scope of the problem (interstate vs local), opportunities for state experimentation, costs of regulatory fragmentation, and international harmonization or trade barrier effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption Against Certain Economic Regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: A particularly demanding burden of proof is required to justify: price controls in competitive markets; production or sales quotas in competitive markets; mandatory uniform quality standards if voluntary standards or disclosure suffice; and controls on entry into employment or production (with limited exceptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these regulatory types skeptically and document why less intrusive alternatives are inadequate; note exceptions (e.g., health/safety testing, common property management).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and Analyze a Baseline
rubrics_metrics.description: Benefits and costs are defined in comparison with a clearly stated alternative—normally a 'no action' baseline; comparisons to a 'next best' alternative are also useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State baseline clearly, and estimate incremental effects of each alternative relative to the baseline or to the closest less-stringent alternative as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain Causal Link Between Rule Requirements and Expected Benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain how the actions required by the rule are linked to the expected benefits (e.g., how additional safety equipment will reduce safety risks) for the proposed action and for each alternative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide mechanism or chain-of-events arguments, quantify where possible, and include similar analysis for each alternative considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify Ancillary Benefits and Undesirable Side-Effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify expected undesirable side-effects and ancillary benefits of the proposed regulatory action and the alternatives, and include them with direct benefits and costs as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify and monetize where feasible; include qualitative discussion of important non-monetized ancillary effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include Non-Quantified as well as Quantified Benefits and Costs
rubrics_metrics.description: A complete regulatory analysis includes a discussion of both quantified (and monetized) and non-quantified benefits and costs; non-quantified outcomes must be identified so policymakers can compare them with monetary estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When non-quantified effects are important, carry out threshold (break-even) analysis and indicate which non-quantified effects are most important and why.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold / Break-Even Analysis for Non-Quantified Effects
rubrics_metrics.description: If important benefits or costs cannot be monetized, conduct a threshold analysis to answer how small the value of non-quantified benefits (or how large non-quantified costs) must be before the rule yields zero net benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use threshold analysis to show potential significance of non-quantified factors and to help decision makers understand how such factors could alter rankings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider a Range of Alternative Regulatory Approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Once Federal action is appropriate, agencies should consider alternative regulatory approaches and explore modifications of regulation attributes to identify appropriate alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preliminarily eliminate some alternatives, but select a manageable set for detailed analysis, balancing thoroughness against practical limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different Choices Defined by Statute
rubrics_metrics.description: When a statute establishes a regulatory requirement and the agency considers a more stringent standard, examine benefits and costs of reasonable alternatives reflecting the range of statutory discretion, including the specific statutory requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include statutory minimums as options in the alternatives set for comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different Compliance Dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze alternative timing/compliance dates because implementation timing can materially affect net benefits and costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider lead times for industry adjustments, biological/ecological delays, and phased approaches that may lower overall costs or preserve benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different Enforcement Methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare compliance/enforcement alternatives (on-site inspections, periodic reporting, penalties, random monitoring, parametric monitoring) in terms of costs and effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the enforcement framework that provides appropriate incentives at least cost while ensuring compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different Degrees of Stringency
rubrics_metrics.description: Study alternative levels of regulatory stringency to understand relationships between stringency and magnitude/distribution of benefits and costs among groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate marginal benefits and marginal costs as stringency changes; consider incremental analysis between successively more stringent options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different Requirements for Different Sized Firms
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider tailoring requirements by firm size based on differences in compliance costs or benefits; remember significant impacts on many small entities trigger Regulatory Flexibility Act requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid inefficient burden shifting to most productive firms and consult small business guidance/Counsel for Advocacy where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different Requirements for Different Geographic Regions
rubrics_metrics.description: Where benefits and costs vary regionally, consider setting differential regional requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess regional heterogeneity and whether regional tailoring improves net benefits without unacceptable complexity or national fragmentation costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer Performance Standards Over Design Standards When Appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Performance standards, which express requirements in terms of outcomes rather than means, generally provide regulated parties flexibility to achieve objectives cost-effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for cost savings from flexibility and for costs of monitoring and ensuring compliance under performance standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider Market-Oriented Approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Explore economic incentive alternatives—fees, penalties, subsidies, marketable permits, changes in liability or property rights, bonds/insurance/warranties—as potentially lower-cost means to achieve objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate approaches like averaging, banking, and trading (ABT) for cost savings while checking for unacceptable local outcomes (e.g., hot spots).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider Informational Measures Before Regulation for Information Problems
rubrics_metrics.description: If the problem stems from inadequate or asymmetric information, evaluate informational remedies (standardized testing/rating systems, mandatory disclosure, government provision of information) as often preferred alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess costs (gathering, communicating, displacement of other information) and potential for misinterpretation; where uncertain, consider least intrusive informational measure sufficient to accomplish objective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Benefit-Cost Analysis (BCA) Appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: BCA expresses benefits and costs in monetary units to evaluate different regulatory options using a common measure; it should be performed for all major rulemakings except where primary benefits are health/safety and cannot be monetized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure incremental benefits and costs of successively more stringent alternatives to identify the alternative that maximizes net benefits; do not rely on benefit-cost ratios alone to judge net benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Cost-Effectiveness Analysis (CEA) Appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: CEA compares regulatory actions when the primary benefits are improved public health and safety (or another single primary outcome) and a valid effectiveness measure exists; perform CEA for major rulemakings with health/safety outcomes and also BCA where monetization is possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer incremental cost-effectiveness comparisons to averages; beware of misleading results when effectiveness measures do not capture variability or when multiple outcomes exist; integrate outcomes into single index only with careful weighting or monetization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct Cost and Effectiveness Measures Carefully and Consistently
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure costs include all relevant societal costs (public and private) and that effectiveness measures capture final outcomes (lives saved, life-years saved) rather than intermediate outputs where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid double-counting; if monetary ancillary benefits can be estimated, subtract them from gross costs to produce net-cost estimates; explain choice of effectiveness measure and its limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incremental vs Average Comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Use incremental comparisons (incremental net benefits or incremental cost-effectiveness) between successively more stringent options rather than relying on averages or ratios that can be misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eliminate dominated alternatives (by strong/weak dominance) and be explicit about whether alternatives are mutually exclusive or combinable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of Non-Monetized Benefits and Costs in BCA/CEA
rubrics_metrics.description: When important benefits or costs cannot be expressed in monetary units, describe them qualitatively, assess their potential importance, and consider threshold analysis; where partial monetization is possible, incorporate monetized ancillaries into net cost calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge uncertainty and potential for non-monetized factors to change ranking of alternatives; explain reasons for designating non-quantified factors as important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present Alternative Estimates for Valuing Mortality Risk
rubrics_metrics.description: When developing estimates for reductions in premature mortality risk, present alternative primary estimates (e.g., differing VSL values) to reflect uncertainty in valuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclose choices and present sensitivity analyses showing how different mortality valuations affect net benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and Documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: A good analysis is transparent: state assumptions (time horizon, discount rates), provide sensitivity analysis, and make clear how estimates and conclusions were derived so a qualified third party can review them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide specific references to all data sources, appendices with model documentation, results of formal sensitivity/uncertainty analyses, and an executive summary including a standardized accounting statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of Time and Discounting
rubrics_metrics.description: Present undiscounted streams of benefit and cost estimates for each year of the analytic time horizon, and present annualized benefits and costs using real discount rates of 3% and 7%; report all monetized effects in 2001 dollars and convert other years using the GDP deflator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start annualized streams in the year the final rule begins to have effects even if implementation is delayed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of Risk, Uncertainty, and Sensitivity Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide expected-value estimates and distributions where possible; when only bounds are provided, use 95% and 5% confidence bounds if possible; perform sensitivity analyses to show how results vary with plausible changes in assumptions and inputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where results are sensitive (e.g., sign of net benefits changes), make alternative assumptions explicit and carry out further analyses to justify choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume Risk Neutrality Unless Justified Otherwise
rubrics_metrics.description: In general, analysts should assume risk neutrality in BCA; if a different risk preference assumption is adopted, explain and justify it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make hidden assumptions explicit and analyze methods carefully for embedded assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision and Rounding of Estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported estimates should reflect appropriate precision; the level of rounding should communicate precision (e.g., $220 million implies rounding to nearest $10 million).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose rounding that matches realistic precision and explicitly document implied precision ranges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate Reporting of Transfers vs Welfare Effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Report transfers separately and avoid misclassifying transfer payments as benefits or costs; distinguish transfers caused by Federal budget actions from transfers between non-governmental parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as many categories as necessary to describe major redistributive effects; report transfers separately so policymakers understand redistributive vs efficiency impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report Distributional Effects on State/Local/Tribal Governments, Small Business, Wages, and Economic Growth
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify portions of benefits, costs, and transfers received by State, local, and tribal governments; to the extent feasible, identify effects on small businesses, wages, and economic growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that rules with annual costs under $1 billion are likely to have minimal effects on economic growth; disclose material distributional impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting Statement with Benefit and Cost Tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide an accounting statement with tables reporting benefit and cost estimates for each major final rule using categories: monetized, quantified but not monetized, and qualitative but not quantified or monetized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid double-counting across categories; present annual streams and annualized estimates, add footnotes for documentation/warnings, and follow suggested formats where provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantifying and Monetizing Benefits and Costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop quantitative estimates and convert them to dollar amounts when possible; measure physical units if monetization is infeasible and describe qualitatively where measurement is impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make monetization efforts where possible; if not possible, be explicit about limits and provide best available quantitative or qualitative assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision on Reporting Uncertainty Distributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Where distributions about estimates exist, present expected values and, when only upper/lower bounds are supplied, provide 95% and 5% confidence bounds if feasible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed distributions are encouraged but not required in the main text; make them available upon request and add explanatory footnotes as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialized Statutory and Executive Requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of and comply with analytic requirements imposed by law and Executive Orders—examples include the Regulatory Flexibility Act (small entities), Unfunded Mandates Act, Paperwork Reduction Act, Information Quality Guidelines, NEPA, EO 13045 (children), and EO 13211 (energy impacts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare and incorporate required analyses/statements (e.g., RFA, written statement under Unfunded Mandates Act, Statement of Energy Effects) and consult appropriate offices (e.g., agency CIO, CEQ, SBA Chief Counsel for Advocacy) for guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Flexibility Analysis for Small Entities
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Regulatory Flexibility Act, prepare a proposed and final regulatory flexibility analysis if the rule could have a significant impact on a substantial number of small entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult agency guidelines and the Chief Counsel for Advocacy of the SBA; consider posting the RFA online and, for SBREFA-covered rules, conduct required small business consultation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unfunded Mandates Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Unfunded Mandates Act, prepare a written statement about benefits and costs prior to issuing proposed or final rules that may result in aggregate expenditures by governments or the private sector of $100 million or more in any one year (adjusted for inflation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Your Executive Order 12866 analytical work may satisfy many of these requirements—coordinate analyses accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paperwork and Information Collection Burdens (PRA Compliance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether rulemaking will create information collection, paperwork, or recordkeeping burdens subject to the Paperwork Reduction Act and justify the practical utility of required information; obtain OMB approval when required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate with agency CIO and seek valid OMB control numbers for collections imposed on 10 or more persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information Quality Standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Data and analysis used to support rules must meet Information Quality Law and agency/OMB quality standards for disseminated information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow agency information quality guidelines and consult OMB Statistical and Science Policy Branch for assistance where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: NEPA and Environmental Impact Considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Comply with NEPA where applicable—prepare environmental impact statements for major Federal actions significantly affecting the human environment and complete NEPA documentation before issuing a final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow CEQ regulations (40 C.F.R. 1500-1508) and associated guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Children's Health and Safety Impacts (EO 13045)
rubrics_metrics.description: For substantive rulemakings likely to be economically significant and concerning environmental health/safety risks that may disproportionately affect children, provide an evaluation of the effects on children and explain why the planned regulation is preferable to other feasible alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address disproportionate risks to children 'to the extent permitted by law and appropriate, and consistent with the agency's mission.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Energy Impacts Statement (EO 13211)
rubrics_metrics.description: Significant energy actions require a Statement of Energy Effects detailing any adverse effects on energy supply, distribution, or use and reasonable alternatives, and require publication of the statement or a summary in notices of proposed and final rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow OMB Memorandum 01-27 for implementation guidance and include required detail on supply disruptions, price effects, and reliance on foreign supplies where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Summary and Standardized Accounting Statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Include an executive summary that contains a standardized accounting statement summarizing monetized and non-monetized benefits and costs for each alternative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the suggested accounting statement format and include footnotes, warnings, and references to appendices for detailed documentation.
